newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada cuts key rate to 3.75 percent.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada cuts key rate to 3.75 percent.

text.p: The Bank of Canada on Wednesday lowered its key bank rate by a quarter point to 3.75 percent, bringing interest rates in Canada to their lowest level in almost 40 years.
Despite the cut -- the ninth by the central bank in 1996 -- analysts said the Bank of Canada could slash rates further this year if there were more signs of economic weakness.

"You really can't rule out another move here because if the data doesn't shape up well, they're going to cut again. And it's perfectly justified by the fundamentals," said Lehman Brothers economist Michael Gregory.
The latest cut quickly prompted Canada's six big commercial banks to lower their prime lending rates to 5.25 percent from 5.50 percent, the lowest level since early 1959.
Canadian financial markets showed little reaction to the rate cut. Stocks, T-bills, bonds and the Canadian dollar ended little changed from Tuesday's close.
The Bank of Canada has cut rates by 4-1/2 points since May 1995. Its previous rate cut was on Oct. 2. Eight of its cuts this year have been independent of action by the U.S. Federal Reserve.
Canada's bank rate is similar to the U.S. federal funds rates -- an overnight interbank lending rate -- now at 5.25 percent.

In a statement, the Bank of Canada said the cut was meant to keep money flowing given the recent strength in the Canadian dollar. The stronger dollar can tighten monetary conditions by making the country's exports less attractive.
But disappointing recent economic data likely had more to do with the cut than the dollar's recent appreciation, analysts said.
"That's what the Bank of Canada is worried about here. The forward (economic) momentum that appeared to be taking hold through the summer has proved fleeting," said Lehman's Gregory.

The cut had been widely expected after the government statistical agency, Statistics Canada, said last Friday that Canadian unemployment jumped to a surprisingly high 9.9 percent in September from 9.4 percent in August.

A Statistics Canada report on Wednesday showing a decline in manufacturers' shipments and new orders and an increase in inventories in August confirmed speculation that Canada's economic recovery is weak.

Aggravating concern about the economy is the expected impact of a strike at the Canadian arm of General Motors Corp., which began on Oct. 2. About 26,000 unionized GM Canada workers are on the picket lines.

"It's not so much the direct impact of the strike. It just so happens the negative impact on the economy of the strike is coming after a couple months of pretty dismal news anyway. Therefore, the bank really has no choice here," said Gregory.
